explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The writer says sound judgment and discernment "will be life to your soul…" (Proverbs 3:22). Not a decoration, not a bonus. Life. That's like finding out the oven mitts are also keeping you warm, and I did NOT see that coming.

Light sounds right, friend, and it's a lovely word. But the verse says they "will be life to your soul…" (Proverbs 3:22). The writer picks life, and that's a lot to hand to a few wise habits. I bet plenty of folks reach for light first, so you're in good company.

Strength is a fair guess, friend, since wise habits can feel like muscle. But the text says they "will be life to your soul…" (Proverbs 3:22). Life is the word the writer uses. Strength doesn't show up in that verse at all.

Not quite, friend. The writer says the opposite: "Then you will go on your way in safety, and your foot will not stumble." (Proverbs 3:23). No "now and then" in there. I've tripped over my own mustache plenty, so I'd take this promise in a heartbeat.

That's right, friend. The writer says, "Then you will go on your way in safety, and your foot will not stumble." (Proverbs 3:23). It's tied to holding on to sound judgment and discernment. No stumbling, and no small print about an exception.

Yes, friend. "When you lie down, you will not be afraid…" (Proverbs 3:24). Not afraid at bedtime. No peeking under the bed, no staring at the ceiling and replaying every little thing. I'd sign up for that one TWICE.

I see why you'd think that, friend, but the verse goes the other way. It says, "When you lie down, you will not be afraid…" (Proverbs 3:24). Nobody's sprinting out of bed in this promise. It's a calm one.

Staying on guard sounds like what a careful person would do, friend. But the writer promises, "When you lie down, you will not be afraid…" (Proverbs 3:24). There's no night watch in that verse. Lying down and not being afraid is the whole point.

explanations.answer: The LORD will be his confidence
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The writer says, "for the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from the snare." (Proverbs 3:26). The reason isn't the son's eyesight or his muscles. It's the LORD.

explanations.answer: He will see it coming early
explanations.explanation: Great plan, friend, but "sudden" means it doesn't send a text first. The verse gives a different reason: "for the LORD will be your confidence…" (Proverbs 3:26). The writer points to the LORD, not to the son's early warning.

explanations.answer: He is strong enough to face it
explanations.explanation: I like the confidence, friend, but the writer doesn't put it on the son. He says, "for the LORD will be your confidence…" (Proverbs 3:26). The strength in this verse belongs to the LORD, and the son leans on Him.
Yes, friend. "Do not withhold good from the deserving when it is within your power to act." (Proverbs 3:27). If you can help, help. Don't sit on it like dough you forgot to bake.

Interesting pick, friend, but this verse isn't about scolding. It says, "Do not withhold good from the deserving…" (Proverbs 3:27). The thing not to hold back is good, and that's a much nicer thing to hand out.

Judgment is all over this passage, friend, so I get it. But in this verse the writer says, "Do not withhold good from the deserving…" (Proverbs 3:27). The word is good. It's about helping when you're able.

Not this time, friend. The writer says, "Do not tell your neighbor, 'Come back tomorrow and I will provide'—when you already have the means." (Proverbs 3:28). If you can help today, then help today. Tomorrow is not an excuse.

Right, friend. The writer says, "Do not tell your neighbor, 'Come back tomorrow and I will provide'—when you already have the means." (Proverbs 3:28). The key part is "when you already have the means." If it's in your hands, there's no reason to make them wait.

explanations.answer: He trusts you and lives beside you
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The writer says, "Do not devise evil against your neighbor, for he trustfully dwells beside you." (Proverbs 3:29). Your neighbor feels safe right next door. Plotting against someone like that is a terrible way to thank them.

explanations.answer: He might find out what you did
explanations.explanation: That would be a good reason to worry, friend, but it's not the one given. The verse says, "…for he trustfully dwells beside you." (Proverbs 3:29). The reason is the neighbor's trust, not whether you'd get caught.

explanations.answer: He could pay you back for it
explanations.explanation: Payback is a fair thing to worry about, friend. But the writer doesn't mention it. He says, "…for he trustfully dwells beside you." (Proverbs 3:29). The reason is that the neighbor trusts you, and that's a heavier reason than fear of payback.
Yes, friend. "Do not accuse a man without cause, when he has done you no harm." (Proverbs 3:30). No reason, no harm done, no accusing. Simple as that.

I see the thinking, friend, but the verse isn't about giving a heads-up first. It says, "Do not accuse a man without cause, when he has done you no harm." (Proverbs 3:30). The word is cause. The man did nothing to you.

Mercy is a beautiful word, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The writer says, "Do not accuse a man without cause, when he has done you no harm." (Proverbs 3:30). It's about accusing someone for no reason at all.
That's right, friend. "Do not envy a violent man or choose any of his ways…" (Proverbs 3:31). Two things on the list: don't envy him, and don't pick up his ways. Both are off the shelf.
That's a kind thought, friend, but it isn't what the verse says. It says, "Do not envy a violent man or choose any of his ways…" (Proverbs 3:31). The other thing not to do is envy him.
Warning someone sounds responsible, friend, but this verse doesn't go there. It says, "Do not envy a violent man or choose any of his ways…" (Proverbs 3:31). The second thing not to do is envy him.

That's right, friend. "…for the LORD detests the perverse, but He is a friend to the upright." (Proverbs 3:32). Read that second half again slowly: a friend to the upright. That's a great thing to be called by the LORD.

This one is true, friend. The text says, "…for the LORD detests the perverse, but He is a friend to the upright." (Proverbs 3:32). I know "detests" is a strong word, but the verse also says He is a friend to the upright, and that's the part worth holding on to.
Yes, friend. "He mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble." (Proverbs 3:34). Grace goes to the humble. I've been stuck in a junk drawer, so I'm a pretty good candidate for humble.

Clever folks are impressive, friend, but they're not the ones named. The verse says, "He mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble." (Proverbs 3:34). Grace goes to the humble, whether or not they're clever.
Money gets a lot of attention, friend, but the verse doesn't mention it. It says, "He mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble." (Proverbs 3:34). The humble are the ones who get the grace.
Yes, friend. "The wise will inherit honor, but fools are held up to shame." (Proverbs 3:35). Honor goes in the first blank, and it's the one the wise inherit. Nice pairing.

Right, friend. "The wise will inherit honor, but fools are held up to shame." (Proverbs 3:35). Shame goes in the second blank, and it's what happens to fools. Put the honor and the shame side by side and the pair is clear.
Silence sounds dramatic, friend, but it isn't in the verse. It says, "The wise will inherit honor, but fools are held up to shame." (Proverbs 3:35). The two words you want are honor and shame.

Exile is a heavy word, friend, but this verse doesn't use it. It says, "The wise will inherit honor, but fools are held up to shame." (Proverbs 3:35). Honor and shame are the words that fit the blanks.
Labor is honest work, friend, and I respect it. But it's not what the verse says. "The wise will inherit honor, but fools are held up to shame." (Proverbs 3:35). The blanks are honor and shame.
